expectedText:
CALIFORNIA PAY DATA REPORTING — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET AND COVERED-EMPLOYER SELF-ASSESSMENT
This information sheet describes selected requirements of California's annual pay data reporting law, Government Code section 12999, as it may apply to a private employer such as Acme, Inc. Section 12999 requires certain private employers to submit an annual pay data report to California's Civil Rights Department, covering workforce composition by pay band, job category, race, ethnicity, and sex, and, separately, to submit a related report covering employees supplied through labor contractors. This document is distinct from this project's separate Pay Scale Disclosure and Salary History Ban Information Sheet, which addresses a different obligation — disclosing a position's pay scale to applicants, employees, and in job postings under Labor Code section 432.3 — not the annual workforce data-reporting obligation addressed here.

This section is a self-assessment worksheet, not a determination that Acme, Inc. is or is not required to file a pay data report. Acme, Inc.'s approximate total employee count is stated as 150; the Reporting Year addressed is 2026; and Acme, Inc.'s use, if any, of labor contractors is described as: We use a staffing agency to supply approximately 20 warehouse workers. This information sheet does not itself calculate whether Acme, Inc. met the 100-employee threshold described below, does not itself prepare or submit any report on Acme, Inc.'s behalf, and does not itself satisfy any filing, recordkeeping, or disclosure duty Section 12999 may impose.

WHICH EMPLOYERS MUST FILE A PAY DATA REPORT, AND THE FILING DEADLINE
California law requires a private employer that has 100 or more employees to submit a pay data report to the department on or before the second Wednesday of May 2023, and on or before the second Wednesday of May of each year thereafter. The report covers the prior calendar year, which the statute designates the “Reporting Year.” The statute's recurring filing duty runs to “the department,” meaning California's Civil Rights Department, and its own text does not state that an employer with fewer than 100 employees is subject to this particular filing duty.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "On or before the second Wednesday of May 2023, and on or before the second Wednesday of May of each year thereafter, a private employer that has 100 or more employees shall submit a pay data report to the department covering the prior calendar year, which, for purposes of this section, shall be referred to as the “Reporting Year.”"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12999(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text, version effective Jan. 1, 2026 through Jan. 1, 2027, added by Stats. 2025, Ch. 760, Sec. 1), California Government Code, pay data report filing threshold and annual deadline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12999.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Government Code section 12999(a)(1)), used as real evidence of California's pay-data-report filing threshold and deadline — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. The citation below is a single paragraph of a single statutory subdivision, not a composite of independent sources. Government Code section 12999 currently exists in two chaptered, time-phased versions from the same 2025 enacting bill: the version quoted here (added by Stats. 2025, Ch. 760, Sec. 1) is effective January 1, 2026 and, by its own terms, remains in effect only until January 1, 2027, when it is automatically repealed and superseded by a differently worded version (added by Sec. 2 of the same bill) that becomes operative that date; a separate clause in this information sheet addresses the one respect in which that later version differs from the text quoted here. This clause was checked against the text confirmed operative as of the checked date above; it does not itself count any employer's employees, does not itself determine that any particular employer met or did not meet the 100-employee threshold for any particular Reporting Year, and is informational only.

SEPARATE REPORT FOR EMPLOYEES HIRED THROUGH LABOR CONTRACTORS
Separately from the general pay data report, California law requires a private employer that has 100 or more employees hired through labor contractors within the prior calendar year to submit a separate pay data report to the department, covering those labor-contractor-supplied employees for that prior calendar year. The employer must also disclose on that report the ownership names of all labor contractors used to supply employees, and the statute places a corresponding duty on the labor contractor itself to supply all necessary pay data to the employer. Any demographic information gathered by an employer or a labor contractor under this section must be collected and stored separately from employees' personnel records.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "a private employer that has 100 or more employees hired through labor contractors within the prior calendar year shall submit a separate pay data report to the department covering the employees hired through labor contractors in the prior calendar year. The private employer shall also disclose on the pay data report the ownership names of all labor contractors used to supply employees. A labor contractor shall supply all necessary pay data to the private employer."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12999(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text, version effective Jan. 1, 2026 through Jan. 1, 2027, added by Stats. 2025, Ch. 760, Sec. 1), California Government Code, separate pay data report for labor-contractor employees (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12999.)
  "Any demographic information gathered by an employer or labor contractor pursuant to this section shall be collected and stored separately from employees’ personnel records."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12999(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text, version effective Jan. 1, 2026 through Jan. 1, 2027, added by Stats. 2025, Ch. 760, Sec. 1), California Government Code, separate storage of demographic information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12999.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Government Code section 12999(a)(2) and (a)(3)), used as real evidence of the labor-contractor pay data reporting duty — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. Both citations below are paragraphs of a single statutory subdivision, (a), of one section; they are treated here as one source describing one connected labor-contractor reporting duty, not as independent corroborating sources. This duty was added to Section 12999 by Senate Bill 1162 of the 2021–22 Regular Session and persists, with the wording quoted here, in the version of the section confirmed operative as of the checked date above. This clause does not itself determine that any particular employer used, or did not use, a labor contractor within the meaning of this section, and does not itself determine that any particular employer's labor-contractor pay data report was or was not filed, complete, or accurate.

REQUIRED CONTENTS OF THE PAY DATA REPORT: JOB CATEGORIES, PAY BANDS, AND CALCULATION METHOD
California law specifies what the pay data report must contain. It must report the number of employees by race, ethnicity, and sex within each of ten listed job categories (currently: executive or senior level officials and managers; first or mid-level officials and managers; professionals; technicians; sales workers; administrative support workers; craft workers; operatives; laborers and helpers; and service workers). It must also report the number of employees by race, ethnicity, and sex whose annual earnings fall within each of the pay bands used by the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics in its Occupational Employment Statistics survey, and, within each job category, the median and mean hourly rate for each combination of race, ethnicity, and sex. To generate these numbers, the employer must create a “snapshot” counting individuals in each job category, by race, ethnicity, and sex, employed during a single pay period of the employer's choice between October 1 and December 31 of the Reporting Year, and must calculate each snapshot employee's total earnings as shown on that employee's Form W-2 for the entire Reporting Year, tabulating how many employees' W-2 earnings fell within each pay band. The report must further include the total hours worked by each employee counted in each pay band during the Reporting Year, and the employer's North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) code.

ALREADY-ENACTED CHANGE TAKING EFFECT JANUARY 1, 2027: NEW JOB CATEGORY LIST
California has already enacted a further change to Government Code section 12999 that is not yet in effect. The version of the section described elsewhere in this information sheet remains in effect only until January 1, 2027, when it is automatically repealed by its own terms. On that same date, a second, already-chaptered version of the section becomes operative and replaces the current ten-item job-category list with a different, longer list of job categories for purposes of the race/ethnicity/sex headcount required by subdivision (b)(1) — for example, “chief executives” and “management occupations, except chief executives” as separate categories, along with categories such as computer and mathematical occupations, legal occupations, and health care support occupations, among others. The remainder of the reporting scheme described in this information sheet — the 100-employee threshold, the filing deadline, the labor-contractor report, the pay-band and snapshot methodology, and the penalty structure — is not altered by this already-enacted change.

PENALTIES FOR FAILING TO FILE, AND HOW THEY ARE ASSESSED
If the department does not receive a required pay data report from an employer, California law authorizes the department to seek a court order requiring the employer to comply, together with the department's costs of seeking that order. Upon the department's request, a court shall impose a civil penalty of up to $100 per employee on an employer that fails to file the required report, and up to $200 per employee for a subsequent failure to file. Any such penalty is payable to the Civil Rights Enforcement and Litigation Fund. If an employer is unable to submit a complete and accurate report because a labor contractor did not provide required pay data, the court may apportion an appropriate share of penalties to that labor contractor instead.

If the employer is unable to submit a complete and accurate report because a labor contractor has not provided the pay data as required under paragraph (2) of subdivision (a), the court may apportion an appropriate amount of penalties to any labor contractor that has failed to provide the pay data to the employer."

CONFIDENTIALITY OF FILED DATA, RECORDKEEPING, AND KEY STATUTORY DEFINITIONS
California law restricts what the department and the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement may do with individually identifiable information submitted in a pay data report: it is unlawful for an officer or employee of either agency to make that information public before an investigation or enforcement proceeding involving it has begun, and even then only to the extent necessary for that proceeding. Individually identifiable information submitted under this section is treated as confidential and is not subject to disclosure under the California Public Records Act. The department must maintain pay data reports for not less than 10 years. The statute also defines three key terms for purposes of this section: an “employee” is an individual on an employer's payroll, including a part-time individual, for whom the employer must withhold federal social security taxes; a “labor contractor” is an individual or entity that supplies, with or without a contract, a client employer with workers to perform labor within the client employer's usual course of business; and an “establishment” is an economic unit producing goods or services.

SELF-ASSESSMENT SUMMARY AND SIGNATURE
Acme, Inc. summarizes its self-assessment under this information sheet as follows:

Reporting Year addressed: 2026

It does not itself determine that Acme, Inc. is, or is not, required to file a pay data report or a separate labor-contractor pay data report under Government Code section 12999 for the stated Reporting Year, and it does not itself prepare, review, or submit any such report.

expectedJSON.body: California has already enacted a further change to Government Code section 12999 that is not yet in effect. The version of the section described elsewhere in this information sheet remains in effect only until January 1, 2027, when it is automatically repealed by its own terms. On that same date, a second, already-chaptered version of the section becomes operative and replaces the current ten-item job-category list with a different, longer list of job categories for purposes of the race/ethnicity/sex headcount required by subdivision (b)(1) — for example, “chief executives” and “management occupations, except chief executives” as separate categories, along with categories such as computer and mathematical occupations, legal occupations, and health care support occupations, among others. The remainder of the reporting scheme described in this information sheet — the 100-employee threshold, the filing deadline, the labor-contractor report, the pay-band and snapshot methodology, and the penalty structure — is not altered by this already-enacted change.

expectedJSON.body: If the department does not receive a required pay data report from an employer, California law authorizes the department to seek a court order requiring the employer to comply, together with the department's costs of seeking that order. Upon the department's request, a court shall impose a civil penalty of up to $100 per employee on an employer that fails to file the required report, and up to $200 per employee for a subsequent failure to file. Any such penalty is payable to the Civil Rights Enforcement and Litigation Fund. If an employer is unable to submit a complete and accurate report because a labor contractor did not provide required pay data, the court may apportion an appropriate share of penalties to that labor contractor instead.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12999(f) (California Legislative Information text, version effective Jan. 1, 2026 through Jan. 1, 2027, added by Stats. 2025, Ch. 760, Sec. 1)
citations.cite: California Government Code, civil penalty for failure to file a pay data report
citations.quote: Upon request by the department, a court shall impose a civil penalty not to exceed one hundred dollars ($100) per employee upon any employer who fails to file the required report and not to exceed two hundred dollars ($200) per employee upon any employer for a subsequent failure to file the required report. Any penalty under this subdivision shall be payable to the Civil Rights Enforcement and Litigation Fund established under Section 12907. If the employer is unable to submit a complete and accurate report because a labor contractor has not provided the pay data as required under paragraph (2) of subdivision (a), the court may apportion an appropriate amount of penalties to any labor contractor that has failed to provide the pay data to the employer.

The citation below is a single paragraph of a single statutory subdivision, not a composite of independent sources. This clause does not identify any reported court decision applying this penalty range, an honest gap disclosed rather than resolved by assumption. This clause does not itself determine that any particular employer has or has not filed a required report, does not calculate any penalty amount, and is informational only.

expectedJSON.body: California law restricts what the department and the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement may do with individually identifiable information submitted in a pay data report: it is unlawful for an officer or employee of either agency to make that information public before an investigation or enforcement proceeding involving it has begun, and even then only to the extent necessary for that proceeding. Individually identifiable information submitted under this section is treated as confidential and is not subject to disclosure under the California Public Records Act. The department must maintain pay data reports for not less than 10 years. The statute also defines three key terms for purposes of this section: an “employee” is an individual on an employer's payroll, including a part-time individual, for whom the employer must withhold federal social security taxes; a “labor contractor” is an individual or entity that supplies, with or without a contract, a client employer with workers to perform labor within the client employer's usual course of business; and an “establishment” is an economic unit producing goods or services.
